headline: The West Cut Still Has the Deepest Water in the System — and Everything's Using It
subhead: Moriches Inlet's channel bend keeps holding cooler water and moving bait while the flats on both sides go soft and warm.
body_markdown:
I ran the inlet on the last of the outgoing Thursday afternoon and watched the sounder tell me something I already suspected — the west cut, off the tip of Cupsogue, is still scoured out to 14, 15 feet where it's been running 11-12 most of the summer. That's the storm-cut behavior this inlet has been doing since the '92 nor'easter reshaped the whole system, and it hasn't stopped rearranging itself since. Every time we get a stretch of strong ebb without much onshore push, that west bend digs a little deeper and pulls a little more current through it, and every bit of bait and every fish that wants moving water funnels right into that slot.

That's exactly why the fluke bite, such as it is, has narrowed down to almost nothing but structure water. The open bay flats — inside Pattersquash, off Senix Creek, up toward East Moriches — are sitting in the mid-70s by afternoon and the fluke have abandoned them. What's left are fish stacked on the channel bends and the deeper edges tight to the jetty rocks on both the Cupsogue and Westhampton sides, where the tide keeps water moving and a few degrees cooler than the sun-baked flats. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along that west cut edge on the last two hours of the ebb, working the drop where 8 feet falls into 14, and it's been good for keeper-class fish in the 18-20 inch range, mixed with plenty of shorts you have to sort through. It's not a fast bite. I'm marking maybe one keeper for every eight or ten drifts through there, but that's about what you should expect from this pattern in late July — the fish are concentrated, not abundant, and you need to be running the exact seam or you're just towing plastic through empty water.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal on us, same story as everywhere else on the South Shore right now with surface temps sitting where they are. Daytime, they're holding deep in that same west cut and along the training rocks, using the current break as shade and an ambush lane, and they will not commit to anything moving during daylight unless it's dead low light. Where it's paying off is after dark, working the inlet on the change of tide with eels — I've had my best luck free-lining a live eel off the jetty rocks on the Cupsogue side starting about an hour before the tide turns and running through the first hour of the flood, when the current slows enough for the eel to swim naturally but there's still enough push to keep bait pinned against the rocks. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in that same stretch, especially where the channel bends hardest around the old scour hole, have been picking off a few better fish too — nothing huge, mostly mid-20s to low 30s, but they're there and they're eating with some consistency once the sun's down.

Bluefish are the one thing that doesn't care what the calendar says or what the bottom's doing — they're riding bunker schools up and down the ocean beach from Pikes Beach through Cupsogue, and when those pods get pinned against the bar, it gets loud fast. I watched a blitz Tuesday morning off the Cupsogue day-use beach that lasted maybe twenty minutes, birds working hard, blues busting bunker right in the wash, and anyone standing there with a metal-lip swimmer or a bucktail with a wide profile was hooked up instantly. That's the same pattern we flagged holding through the week if the wind stayed cooperative, and it has — no real wind shift, so the blitz windows keep showing up in that same stretch of beach most mornings on the incoming tide, usually within an hour or two of first light. It shuts off just as fast as it starts once the bunker push offshore or the blues move down the beach, so you can't sleep on it.

Weakfish are still showing, but sparingly, and mostly as a bonus rather than a target. A few guys working bucktails and Gulp swimming shad in the deeper holes off Tuthill Point and in the channel bends up toward East Moriches have picked off a weakfish or two mixed in with the fluke, generally on the last of the ebb when that deeper water is moving hardest. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now, but if you're fishing the same structure that's holding fluke, don't be shocked if something with a softer mouth and a little more color grabs the jig.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, and that means more current through this system over the next week, which should sharpen everything up in the inlet — deeper scour on that west cut, harder push through the training rocks, and a better window for the bass bite after dark as the tide swings with more authority. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest like it has been, I'd keep working that same west cut edge on the ebb for fluke, hit the Cupsogue beach at first light for blues, and save the eels for the turn of the tide after dark. If we get a blow out of the east, that inlet will reshape again — it always does — and I'll be back out there with the sounder finding out where the new deep water is.
